draft.title: Identifying health priorities
card: A health priority is an issue that governments and health services give extra attention and funding. Not every health issue can be a priority, so criteria are used to choose.
Burden
how common an issue is and how much it costs. Cost includes harm to people, such as illness and early death, and the cost to the health system and the economy.
Groups affected
issues that fall more heavily on some groups than others can be made priorities, so that the gap between groups can be reduced.
Preventable
if many cases can be avoided, for example by changing risk factors, then action is likely to give a large gain for the money spent.
draft.remember: Priorities are chosen by how common and costly an issue is, who it hits hardest and how much of it can be prevented.

a.q: Which reason would best support making a health issue a national priority?
opts: It is common, costly and many cases can be prevented
It is rare, but each case is reported in the news
It is common, but nothing can be done to prevent it
It affects people in only one town and costs little
a.why: Being common, costly and preventable covers the criteria for a priority, and action can make a large difference. A common issue that cannot be prevented meets only one criterion, so it is a weaker case.
a.clue: Look for the option that meets the most criteria.

b.q: Health officials in Australia compare two issues. Issue X is fairly common and costly, and half of cases can be prevented. Issue Y is as common and costly, but hardly any cases can be prevented. Why might X be given higher priority?
opts: Action on X is likely to avoid more illness for the money
X must cost the health system more than Y does
Y affects fewer groups than X does
Y is not a health issue if it cannot be prevented
b.why: X and Y are equally common and costly, so the difference is how preventable they are. More preventable cases means action on X is likely to give a larger gain. The cost is stated as the same, so the cost option is wrong.
b.clue: What is different between X and Y in the question?

a.best: It is common, costly and many cases can be prevented

b.best: Action on X is likely to avoid more illness for the money

problems.detail: Too easy for Year 12. The right option is the only one that meets any criterion positively, and the distractors (rare but in the news, one town and costs little) are obviously weak, so it tests little beyond recognition.
The right option is the only one with a hedge ('is likely to'), while the distractors are absolute ('must', 'is not'). A test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.

proposal.remember: Priorities are chosen by how common and costly an issue is, who it hits hardest and how much of it can be prevented.

a.q: A report finds a disease is three times as common in remote areas as in cities. Which criterion does this evidence support?
opts: Which groups the issue affects most
How common the issue is across the population
How many cases of the issue can be prevented
How much the issue costs the health system
a.why: The report compares two groups and shows the disease falls more heavily on one of them. That is the groups affected criterion. It does not give the overall rate for all Australians, so it is not evidence of how common the issue is across the population.
a.clue: Is the report about the whole population or a gap between groups?

b.q: Health officials in Australia compare two issues. Issue X is fairly common and costly, and half of cases can be prevented. Issue Y is as common and costly, but hardly any cases can be prevented. Why might X be given higher priority?
opts: Action on X can prevent more illness for the money spent
X can cause more illness and cost more than Y does
X can fall more heavily on some groups than Y does
Y can be left alone because its cases cannot be prevented
b.why: X and Y are equally common and costly, so the difference is how preventable they are. More preventable cases means action on X is likely to give a larger gain. The question says nothing about groups, and it states the burden is the same, so those options do not explain the choice.
b.clue: What is different between X and Y in the question?

a.best: Which groups the issue affects most

b.best: Action on X can prevent more illness for the money spent
